name: Goldreich's CS Perspective
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: What a Cryptographer Sees That Physicists Miss
lesson.summary: Oded Goldreich, a leading theoretical computer scientist known for his work in cryptography and complexity theory, has offered a more skeptical, computer science grounded view of quantum computing that focuses on how narrow the set of problems with real quantum speedup actually is.
lesson.body:
Most public discussion of quantum computing skepticism comes from physicists worried about hardware: can qubits be kept coherent, can errors be corrected, can a machine with enough qubits actually be built. Oded Goldreich, a theoretical computer scientist well known for foundational work in cryptography and computational complexity, approaches the question from a different angle entirely. His perspective, as it has been expressed in various talks and writings over the years, treats quantum computing less as an engineering project and more as a claim about computational complexity theory, and he has raised pointed questions about how much practical value would actually follow even from a working large scale quantum computer. As with the previous chapter, this book will not attempt to quote him with precision or attribute exact statements, only describe the general shape of a computer science native skepticism that his work represents.

The starting point of this perspective connects directly to narrow problem applicability. From a complexity theory standpoint, the list of problems where a quantum algorithm provides a proven, exponential advantage over the best known classical algorithm is short. Factoring large numbers, the basis of Shor's algorithm, is the headline example, and it matters mainly because of its relevance to breaking certain cryptographic systems. Simulating certain quantum physical systems is another genuine use case. Beyond that, the list of exponential speedups thins out quickly, and many of the more commonly cited "quantum advantage" claims involve either polynomial speedups, which are far less dramatic once real world overhead is accounted for, or narrow academic benchmarks with limited practical relevance.

A computer scientist trained in cryptography also tends to notice something that hardware focused narratives often gloss over: even a fully working, fault tolerant quantum computer would not make computers faster in general, the way a new generation of classical chips does. It would be a specialized coprocessor, useful for a specific, fairly short list of problem types, sitting alongside ordinary classical computers that continue to do essentially all everyday computing. This framing is deliberately deflationary compared to the popular image of quantum computers as a wholesale replacement for classical machines, and it is a useful corrective for students who have absorbed the more sweeping version of the story from popular science coverage.

It is worth being clear that this is a perspective, not a settled consensus, and complexity theory itself is an active research area where the boundaries of quantum advantage are still being mapped out. New problems with proven quantum speedup could still be discovered, and some current uncertainty in complexity theory, such as open questions around the relationship between quantum and classical complexity classes, cuts in favor of humility on both sides of the debate.

What this perspective offers a student is a second, independent lens on the field, arriving at similar caution as physics based skeptics like Laughlin but for entirely different reasons. When a hardware skeptic and a complexity theory skeptic converge on "this may end up being narrower and slower to matter than advertised," even from completely different starting assumptions, that convergence is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as coming from people who simply do not understand the field.
